items.title: The two-sign bilateral shift space, its coding map, and the ball of bounded bilateral real sequences
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#1 (the sign alphabet X={-1,+1}^Z, the shift, and the ball B_R of bounded bilateral sequences)
items.statement:
Write $\Sigma_{\pm}:=\{-1,+1\}$ and

$$X_{\pm}\ :=\ \Sigma_{\pm}^{\mathbb Z}\ =\ \{\,s\ :\ s \text{ is a function } \mathbb Z\to\Sigma_{\pm}\,\},$$

with the function-set convention of [[def-function-space]]; for $s\in X_{\pm}$ write $s_k:=s(k)$. The elements of $X_{\pm}$ are called **two-sign bilateral sequences**.

**Coding correspondence with the published two-symbol space.** Let

$$\varphi:X_{\pm}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z},\qquad \varphi(s)_k:=\frac{s_k+1}{2}\in\{0,1\},$$

and let $X_2:=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb Z}$, $d_2$ and $\sigma_2$ be the set, the metric expression and the shift map of [[def-cm-bilateral-shift-space-and-cylinders]]. The formulas $\varphi(s)_k=(s_k+1)/2$ and $\varphi^{-1}(t)_k=2t_k-1$ define maps $X_{\pm}\to X_2$ and $X_2\to X_{\pm}$ that are inverse to each other, coordinate by coordinate.

**Metric expression on $X_{\pm}$.** Define

$$D_{\pm}(s,t):=d_2\bigl(\varphi(s),\varphi(t)\bigr)\qquad(s,t\in X_{\pm}).$$

Unwinding the series of [[def-cm-bilateral-shift-space-and-cylinders]] and using $|\varphi(s)_k-\varphi(t)_k|=\tfrac12|s_k-t_k|$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ gives the explicit expression

$$D_{\pm}(s,t)=\sum_{k\ge 0}2^{-(k+1)}\,|s_k-t_k|\;+\;\sum_{k\ge 1}2^{-(k+1)}\,|s_{-k}-t_{-k}| .$$

Both series converge by comparison with the geometric series $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}=2$ ([[def-series]], [[thm-geometric-series]], [[def-integer-power]], [[def-abs-value]]), because $|s_k-t_k|\in\{0,2\}$ for every $k$; hence $D_{\pm}(s,t)$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number. Whether $D_{\pm}$ is a metric is **not** asserted here; it is proved in the companion lemma on this page, together with the statement that $\varphi$ is an isometry of $(X_{\pm},D_{\pm})$ onto $(X_2,d_2)$.

**The shift.** The **(bilateral) shift** of $X_{\pm}$ is

$$S_{\pm}:X_{\pm}\longrightarrow X_{\pm},\qquad S_{\pm}(s)_k:=s_{k+1}\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z,\ s\in X_{\pm}).$$

For $m\in\mathbb Z$ its iterate satisfies $S_{\pm}^{m}(s)_k=s_{k+m}$; in particular $S_{\pm}$ is a bijection with inverse $S_{\pm}^{-1}(s)_k=s_{k-1}$, and $S_{\pm}=\varphi^{-1}\circ\sigma_2\circ\varphi$.

**Bounded bilateral sequences.** A function $x:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ is **bounded** when its range $\{x_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Write

$$\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb Z):=\{\,x:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\ :\ x \text{ is bounded}\,\},\qquad \|x\|_{\infty}:=\sup\{\,|x_k|\ :\ k\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

The set $\{|x_k|:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ whose supremum is taken is nonempty and bounded above ([[def-bounded-set]]), so $\|x\|_\infty$ is a well-defined nonnegative real number ([[lem-sup-unique]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]). For $R>0$ put

$$B_R:=\{\,x\in\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb Z)\ :\ \|x\|_{\infty}\le R\,\}.$$

Thus $B_R$ is the closed ball of radius $R$ in the supremum norm, and $\|x\|_\infty\le R$ is by definition the statement that $|x_k|\le R$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-abs-value]]).

items.title: The square-root recurrence $T_s(x)_n = s_n\sqrt{a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}}$ is a contraction of $B_R$ with a unique coded solution
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#1 (radicand bounds, the derivative bound 1/(2L), and the unique coded sequence)
items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad L:=\sqrt{\,a-2R\,}.$$

Let $X_{\pm}$ and $B_R$ be the two-sign shift space and the closed ball of bounded bilateral sequences of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], and for $s\in X_{\pm}$ define

$$T_s:B_R\longrightarrow \mathbb R^{\mathbb Z},\qquad (T_sx)_n:=s_n\sqrt{\,a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}\,}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$

For a nonzero real $r$, define $\operatorname{sign}r:=+1$ when $r>0$ and
$\operatorname{sign}r:=-1$ when $r<0$. Once clause 2 establishes
$T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$, its iterates are defined by
$T_s^0:=\operatorname{id}_{B_R}$ and $T_s^{m+1}:=T_s\circ T_s^m$ for
$m\in\mathbb N$.

Then:

1. $a-2R=(\sqrt a-1)^2-7\ge74$, so $L\ge\sqrt{74}>1$; moreover $a+2R<R^2$, hence $\sqrt{a+2R}<R$;
2. for every $s\in X_{\pm}$ and $x\in B_R$ the radicands $a+x_{n-1}+x_{n+1}$ lie in $[a-2R,a+2R]\subseteq(0,\infty)$, so $T_sx$ is a well-defined bounded sequence with $\|T_sx\|_\infty\le\sqrt{a+2R}<R$; in particular $T_s(B_R)\subseteq B_R$;
3. for all $x,y\in B_R$ and every $s\in X_{\pm}$,

$$\|T_sx-T_sy\|_\infty\le\frac1L\,\|x-y\|_\infty,\qquad \frac1L<1 ;$$

4. hence $T_s$ has, for each $s\in X_{\pm}$, exactly one fixed point $x(s)\in B_R$, and for every $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$\operatorname{sign}x_n(s)=s_n,\qquad |x_n(s)|\ge L,\qquad x_{n+1}(s)+x_{n-1}(s)=x_n(s)^2-a .$$
items.strategy: Positivity of the radicand interval, the Lipschitz bound of the square root on [L^2,a+2R], Banach's fixed point theorem on the complete ball, and the sign/recurrence identities at the fixed point.

items.title: Finite symbol windows determine the code: locality of the iterates, coding continuity and injectivity of $h(\sigma)=(x_{-1}(\sigma),x_0(\sigma))$
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#1 (finite-locality of the iterates, error 2R L^{-m}, continuity and injectivity of the coding map)
items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$ and let $R=\sqrt a+3$, $L=\sqrt{a-2R}$, $X_\pm$, $D_\pm$ and $B_R$ be as in [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]] and [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]]. Define the **quadratic phase map**

$$F:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F(x,y):=(y,\;y^2-a-x),$$

and for each $s\in X_\pm$ let $x(s)$ be the unique fixed point of $T_s$ in $B_R$. Define the **coding map**

$$h:X_\pm\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad h(s):=\bigl(x_{-1}(s),\,x_0(s)\bigr).$$

Then:

1. $F$ is a bijection with $F^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,\,x)$, and for every $s\in X_\pm$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$

$$F\bigl(x_{n-1}(s),x_n(s)\bigr)=\bigl(x_n(s),x_{n+1}(s)\bigr);$$

2. **(locality)** for all $m\ge0$, $n\in\mathbb Z$ and $s,t\in X_\pm$: if $s_j=t_j$ for all $j$ with $|j-n|\le m-1$, then $\bigl(T_s^m0\bigr)_n=\bigl(T_t^m0\bigr)_n$, where $T_s^m$ is the $m$-fold iterate and $0$ the zero sequence;
3. **(uniform error)** for all $m\ge0$ and $s\in X_\pm$,

$$\bigl\|T_s^m0-x(s)\bigr\|_\infty\le 2R\,L^{-m};$$

4. **(coding continuity)** if $s,t\in X_\pm$ agree at every coordinate $j$ with $|j|\le m$, then $|x_n(s)-x_n(t)|\le4R\,L^{-m}$ for $n\in\{-1,0\}$, and consequently

$$\bigl\|h(s)-h(t)\bigr\|_2\le4\sqrt2\,R\,L^{-m};$$

in particular $h$ is continuous at every $s\in X_\pm$ ([[def-metric-continuity]]) when $X_\pm$ carries $D_\pm$ and $\mathbb R^2$ the Euclidean metric;

5. **(injectivity)** $h$ is injective.
items.strategy: Induction on m for the window dependence, the Banach a priori error estimate for the uniform tail bound, and the inverse-map sign argument for injectivity.

items.title: Constant codes give the fixed points, and finite nonconstant word codes give homoclinic orbits converging to a fixed point at both ends
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#1 (constant codes, finite-word deviations and their homoclinic limits)
items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$, let $R=\sqrt a+3$, $L=\sqrt{a-2R}$, let $x(s)$ and $h$ be the coded sequence and coding map of [[def-bilateral-symbol-and-bounded-sequence-space]], [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]] and [[lem-symbol-locality-gives-coding-continuity]], and let $F(x,y)=(y,y^2-a-x)$. For $u\in\{-1,+1\}$ write $\bar u\in X_\pm$ for the constant code $\bar u_n:=u$, and put

$$r_u:=1+u\sqrt{a+1},$$

so that $r_+>0>r_-$, and write $W^s,W^u$ for the stable and unstable sets of [[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]. Then:

1. $x_n(\bar u)=r_u$ for every $n$, and $r_u^2=a+2r_u$; consequently $h(\bar u)=(r_u,r_u)$ is a fixed point of $F$;
2. if $s\in X_\pm$ satisfies $s_n=u$ for all $|n|\ge N$ for some $N\ge0$, then

$$F^n\bigl(h(s)\bigr)\longrightarrow(r_u,r_u)\quad\text{as }n\to+\infty\quad\text{and as }n\to-\infty ;$$

3. if moreover $s$ is not the constant code $\bar u$, then $h(s)\ne(r_u,r_u)$, $F^n(h(s))\ne(r_u,r_u)$ for every $n\in\mathbb Z$, and $h(s)\in W^s(r_u,r_u)\cap W^u(r_u,r_u)$; hence $h(s)$ is a homoclinic point of the fixed point $(r_u,r_u)$;
4. distinct codes $s\ne t$ of the kind in clause 2 give distinct points $h(s)\ne h(t)$; in particular the finite-word deviations from the two constant codes produce infinitely many distinct homoclinic points.
items.strategy: Constant codes are fixed by the sign-preserving square-root recurrence; the finite-word deviation has constant tails, and the locality estimate forces convergence of the coded orbit to the corresponding constant fixed point in both time directions.

items.title: Stable and unstable cones, invariant line slopes, stable and unstable sets, and transverse homoclinic points of the quadratic family
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#2 and #3 (cones C^s_k, C^u_k, slope graph transforms, local stable and unstable sets, transverse homoclinic points)
items.statement:
**The quadratic family.** For $a\in\mathbb R$ let

$$F_a:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad F_a(x,y):=(y,\,y^2-a-x),$$

with differential at $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$

$$DF_a(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&2y\end{pmatrix}.$$

The inverse map is

$$F_a^{-1}(x,y)=(x^2-a-y,x),$$

and its differential at $(x,y)$ is

$$D(F_a^{-1})(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}2x&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Here $DF_a(x,y)^{-1}$ denotes the inverse matrix of $DF_a(x,y)$, namely
$\begin{pmatrix}2y&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; it is not the same notation as
$D(F_a^{-1})(x,y)$, which evaluates the derivative of the inverse map at the
point $(x,y)$. All matrices act on column vectors of $\mathbb R^2$
([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

**Complex coordinates and modulus.** Use $\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$,
with real numbers embedded as constant classes and $i:=x+(x^2+1)$, so $i^2=-1$
([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]). This is a field and each element has
a unique form $\alpha+i\beta$ with $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define its modulus by

$$|\alpha+i\beta|:=\sqrt{\alpha^2+\beta^2},$$

where the square root is the unique nonnegative real square root
([[thm-of-square-roots]]). Identify $\mathbb C^2$ with pairs of complex
coordinates; a real matrix acts on it by the same matrix entries, extended
$\mathbb C$-linearly.

**Hyperbolic fixed points.** Let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open, let
$G:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, and let $\bar z\in U\cap V$ satisfy
$G(\bar z)=\bar z$. Its eigenvalues are the numbers $\lambda\in\mathbb C$
for which $DG(\bar z)v=\lambda v$ for some $v\in\mathbb C^2\setminus\{0\}$.
The fixed point $\bar z$ is **hyperbolic** when every such eigenvalue satisfies
$|\lambda|\ne1$. A global $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ is the special
case $U=V=\mathbb R^2$.

**Cones.** Fix $k\in(0,1)$. The **unstable cone** and **stable cone** of aperture $k$ are

$$C^u_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |u|\le k|v|\,\},\qquad C^s_k:=\{\,(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2\ :\ |v|\le k|u|\,\}$$

([[def-abs-value]]); both are closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$, they are closed under multiplication by real scalars, and $C^u_k\cap C^s_k=\{0\}$, because a nonzero vector in the intersection would satisfy $|u|\le k|v|$ and $|v|\le k|u|$, hence $|u|\le k^2|u|<|u|$.

**Slopes.** A line through the origin not contained in the horizontal axis is written uniquely as $\{(hv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $h=u/v$; here $|h|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^u_k$. Similarly a line not contained in the vertical axis is written uniquely as $\{(u,ru):u\in\mathbb R\}$ with the **slope parameter** $r=v/u$, and $|r|\le k$ characterises the lines contained in $C^s_k$.

For real numbers $x,y$ two maps on slope parameters are defined:

$$\Phi_y(h):=\frac{1}{2y-h}\quad(h\ne2y)\quad\text{(forward slope map)},\qquad \Psi_x(r):=\frac{1}{2x-r}\quad(r\ne2x)\quad\text{(backward slope map)}.$$

The intended reading is the graph-transform reading: $DF_a(x,y)$ carries the line
$\{(hv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ at $(x,y)$ to the line
$\{(h'v,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ at $F_a(x,y)$ with $h'=\Phi_y(h)$, and
$D(F_a^{-1})(x,y)$ carries the line $\{(u,ru):u\in\mathbb R\}$ at $(x,y)$
to the line $\{(u,r'u):u\in\mathbb R\}$ at $F_a^{-1}(x,y)$ with
$r'=\Psi_x(r)$. These two statements follow from the displayed matrices and
are proved in the companion lemma on this page, not asserted as part of this
definition.

**Invariant line fields on a sequence.** A **real bilateral sequence** is a function $s:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$; write $s_n:=s(n)$. Put $z_n:=(s_{n-1},s_n)$. An **unstable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^u_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ of lines through the origin of $\mathbb R^2$ such that $DF_a(z_n)$ maps $L^u_n$ onto $L^u_{n+1}$ for every $n$. A **stable line field along $s$** is a family $(L^s_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ such that $D(F_a^{-1})(z_{n+1})$ maps $L^s_{n+1}$ onto $L^s_n$ for every $n$. The latter evaluates the derivative of the inverse map at $z_{n+1}$. When $s$ satisfies $s_{n+1}=s_n^2-a-s_{n-1}$, one has $z_{n+1}=F_a(z_n)$, so these are the source and target orbit points. The displayed matrix conditions also define line families for arbitrary sequences, without asserting that such a sequence is an orbit. Existence and uniqueness of line fields with slopes in $[-k,k]$ for sequences with $|s_n|\ge L$ are proved in the companion lemma on this page.

**Stable and unstable sets.** Let $G:Z\to Z$ be a bijection of a metric
space $(Z,d)$ ([[def-metric-space]]) with fixed point $\bar z$ (so
$G(\bar z)=\bar z$). Put

$$W^s(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^n(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^n(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

$$W^u(\bar z):=\{\,z\in Z\ :\ G^{-n}(z)\ \text{is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^{-n}(z)\to\bar z\ \text{as }n\to\infty\,\},$$

where convergence is that of the metric $d$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]). The
sets $W^s(\bar z)$ and $W^u(\bar z)$ are the **stable set** and the
**unstable set** of $\bar z$.

These orbit-based definitions also apply to a local map. Let $U,V\subseteq
\mathbb R^2$ be open, let $G:U\to V$ be a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, and let
$\bar z\in U\cap V$ satisfy $G(\bar z)=\bar z$. Define $G^0(z):=z$ and
recursively $G^{n+1}(z):=G(G^n(z))$ whenever $G^n(z)\in U$; define
$G^{-n-1}(z):=G^{-1}(G^{-n}(z))$ whenever $G^{-n}(z)\in V$. Then

$$W^s_G(\bar z):=\{z\in U:G^n(z)\text{ is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^n(z)\to\bar z\},$$

$$W^u_G(\bar z):=\{z\in V:G^{-n}(z)\text{ is defined for every }n\ge0\text{ and }G^{-n}(z)\to\bar z\},$$

where convergence is Euclidean metric convergence. The explicit domain clauses
require every forward iterate to lie in $U$ before applying $G$, and every
backward iterate to lie in $V$ before applying $G^{-1}$. In the global case
above every iterate is defined automatically.

A **homoclinic point** is a point in both the stable and unstable sets,
different from the fixed point $\bar z$. For a global bijection on
$\mathbb R^2$ or a local planar diffeomorphism as above, it is
**transverse** when there are $\varepsilon>0$ and $C^1$ maps
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-derivative]])

$$\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2$$

such that $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z$, the stable curve takes values in the
stable set and the unstable curve takes values in the unstable set, both are
injective on $(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ with
$\gamma_s'(0)\ne0\ne\gamma_u'(0)$, and the derivative vectors
$\gamma_s'(0),\gamma_u'(0)\in\mathbb R^2$ are linearly independent. Thus
derivatives and tangent vectors in this definition are taken in the
two-dimensional differentiable setting used by the results on this page; no
derivative is assigned to a curve in an arbitrary metric space. The interval
$(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$ is
that of [[def-interval]].

items.title: Cone invariance and expansion, and convergence of the slope graph transforms to unique invariant stable and unstable line fields
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#2 (cone mapping, expansion by lambda=2L-k, contraction lambda^{-2} of the slope maps)
items.statement:
Let $a\in\mathbb R$, $k\in(0,1)$ and $L\ge2$. Let $s=(s_n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ be a real bilateral sequence with $|s_n|\ge L$ for every $n$, put $z_n:=(s_{n-1},s_n)$, and let $C^u_k$, $C^s_k$, $\Phi_y$, $\Psi_x$, $DF_a$ and $F_a$ be as in [[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]. Write

$$\lambda:=2L-k>1,\qquad \rho:=\lambda^{-2}<1,$$

Assume in addition the aperture condition $k(2L-k)\ge1$, equivalently
$1/\lambda\le k$. This condition is needed for invariance of the stated
cones and slope interval; $L\ge2$ alone does not imply it for arbitrarily
small $k$. Then:

1. **(cone invariance and expansion)** for every $n$: $DF_a(z_n)$ maps $C^u_k$ into itself, and every $(u,v)\in C^u_k$ satisfies

$$\max\bigl(|v|,\,|{-u}+2s_nv|\bigr)\ \ge\ \lambda\,\max(|u|,|v|);$$

and $D(F_a^{-1})(z_n)$ maps $C^s_k$ into itself, with $\max(|2s_{n-1}u-v|,|u|)\ge\lambda\max(|u|,|v|)$ for every $(u,v)\in C^s_k$;
2. **(slope contractions)** for every real $y$ with $|y|\ge L$, the map $\Phi_y$ carries $[-k,k]$ into $[-1/\lambda,1/\lambda]\subseteq[-k,k]$ and satisfies $|\Phi_y(h)-\Phi_y(h')|\le\rho\,|h-h'|$ there; the same holds for $\Psi_x$ for every $|x|\ge L$;
3. **(unstable line field)** define $h^{(0)}_n:=0$ and $h^{(m+1)}_n:=\Phi_{s_{n-1}}\bigl(h^{(m)}_{n-1}\bigr)$ for $m\ge0$. Then $(h^{(m)}_n)_m$ converges for every $n$ to a limit $h_n\in[-k,k]$, uniformly in $n$, and

$$h_{n}=\frac{1}{2s_{n-1}-h_{n-1}}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z);$$

furthermore $DF_a(z_n)$ maps the line $\{(h_nv,v):v\in\mathbb R\}$ onto the line $\{(h_{n+1}v,v)\}$ for every $n$, so the lines form the unique unstable line field along $s$ whose slopes all lie in $[-k,k]$;

items.statement:
Let $\theta\in(0,1)$, $c>0$ and put

$$q:=c\,(\theta+\theta^{-1}),\qquad\text{and assume }q<1 .$$

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let $s\in X_\pm$,
and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $J\times J\subseteq O$. For
$u\in\{-1,+1\}$ let $\widetilde M_u:O\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); write $M_u$ for its
restriction to $J\times J$, assume $M_u(J\times J)\subseteq J$, and suppose
that

$$\bigl|\partial_1M_u\bigr|\le c,\qquad \bigl|\partial_2M_u\bigr|\le c\qquad\text{on }J\times J .$$

Let $(y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a sequence with $y_n\in J$ and let $b_*\in J$ satisfy

$$y_n=M_{s_n}(y_{n-1},y_{n+1})\quad(n\ge1),\qquad y_0=M_{s_0}(b_*,y_1),$$

and assume there is $\bar\rho>0$ with $[y_n-\bar\rho,\,y_n+\bar\rho]\subseteq J$ for every $n\ge0$. Choose $\delta_*>0$ such that

$$[b_*-\delta_*,\,b_*+\delta_*]\subseteq J,\qquad \delta_*<\frac{(1-q)\bar\rho}{c},$$

and put $I:=(b_*-\delta_*,b_*+\delta_*)$. Write

$$\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N):=\Bigl\{\,u:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R\ :\ \|u\|_\theta:=\sup_{n\ge0}\theta^{-n}|u_n|<\infty\,\Bigr\}$$

with metric $\|u-v\|_\theta$, and define its closed ball

$$\mathcal B_{\bar\rho}:=\{u\in\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N):\|u\|_\theta\le\bar\rho\}.$$

For $u\in\mathcal B_{\bar\rho}$ and $b\in I$, put $z_{-1}:=b$ and
$z_k:=y_k+u_k$ for every $k\ge0$, and define $T_b:\mathcal B_{\bar\rho}\to\mathcal B_{\bar\rho}$ by

$$(T_bu)_n:=M_{s_n}\bigl(z_{n-1},z_{n+1}\bigr)-y_n\qquad(n\ge0).$$

Then:

1. $\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ is a complete metric space and $\mathcal B_{\bar\rho}$ is complete in the distance $\|u-v\|_\theta$; for every $b\in I$ the map $T_b$ is a contraction with constant $q<1$, so it has exactly one fixed point $u(b)\in\mathcal B_{\bar\rho}$;
2. for every $b\in I$ one has the a priori bound $\|u(b)\|_\theta\le c\,|b-b_*|/(1-q)$, and the map $b\mapsto u(b)$ is Lipschitz on $I$ with

$$\|u(b')-u(b)\|_\theta\le\frac{c}{1-q}\,|b'-b| ;$$

3. $b\mapsto u(b)$ is continuously differentiable on $I$ into $\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$: with $z^*_k:=y_k+u_k(b)$ for $k\ge0$ and $z^*_{-1}:=b$, the derivative $d(b):=du(b)/db\in\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ is the unique element of $\ell^\infty_\theta(\mathbb N)$ satisfying

$$d_n(b)=\partial_1M_{s_n}(z^*_{n-1},z^*_{n+1})\,d_{n-1}(b)+\partial_2M_{s_n}(z^*_{n-1},z^*_{n+1})\,d_{n+1}(b)\quad(n\ge1),$$

$$d_0(b)=\partial_1M_{s_0}\bigl(b,z^*_1\bigr)+\partial_2M_{s_0}\bigl(b,z^*_1\bigr)\,d_1(b),\qquad d_{-1}(b):=1,$$

and $\|d(b)\|_\theta\le c/(1-q)$;
4. consequently the local phase curve

$$\gamma(b):=\bigl(b,\;y_0+u_0(b)\bigr)$$

defined for $b\in I$ is $C^1$ with $\gamma'(b)=(1,d_0(b))$, and so $|d_0(b)|\le c/(1-q)$.

items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$ and put $R:=\sqrt a+3$, so that $R\ge13$. Let $0<\varepsilon<1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $[-R-1,R+1]^2\subseteq U$, and let $G=(A,B):U\to\mathbb R^2$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) whose components satisfy, on the closed square $S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2$,

$$|A(x,y)-y|\le\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial_xA(x,y)|\le\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial_yA(x,y)-1|\le\varepsilon,$$

$$|B(x,y)-(y^2-a-x)|\le\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial_xB(x,y)+1|\le\varepsilon,\qquad |\partial_yB(x,y)-2y|\le\varepsilon .$$

Then:

1. for every $(q,q')\in[-R,R]^2$ the equation $A(q,v)=q'$ has exactly one solution $v=V(q,q')\in[-R-1,R+1]$, and this defines a map $V:[-R,R]^2\to[-R-1,R+1]$;
2. $V$ is of class $C^1$ on $[-R,R]^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), with

$$\partial_qV(q,q')=-\frac{\partial_xA(q,V)}{A_y(q,V)},\qquad \partial_{q'}V(q,q')=\frac{1}{\partial_yA(q,V)};$$

3. $V$ satisfies the uniform estimates

$$\bigl|V(q,q')-q'\bigr|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \bigl|\partial_qV(q,q')\bigr|\le\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon},\qquad \bigl|\partial_{q'}V(q,q')-1\bigr|\le\frac{\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon}$$

for every $(q,q')\in[-R,R]^2$.

items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#4 (the perturbed defect e, sign margins, unique roots M_s and the bounds d=(1+eta)/(2l-eta))
items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad l:=\sqrt a-3\ge7,\qquad S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2 .$$

Let $0<\varepsilon\le1/6$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $S\subseteq U$, and let $G=(A,B):U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^2$ map satisfying the closeness hypotheses of [[lem-close-map-first-component-has-uniform-inverse]] on $S$ with constant $\varepsilon$; let $V:[-R,R]^2\to[-R-1,R+1]$ be its inverse branch. Define the **defect**

$$e(u,v,w):=-\bigl(V(v,w)-w\bigr)+2v\,\bigl(V(u,v)-v\bigr)+\bigl(V(u,v)-v\bigr)^2+B\bigl(u,V(u,v)\bigr)-\bigl(V(u,v)^2-a-u\bigr)$$

for $(u,v,w)\in[-R,R]^3$, and put

$$P_{u,w}(v):=v^2-a-u-w+e(u,v,w),\qquad (u,v,w)\in[-R,R]^3 .$$

Then:

1. $e$ is of class $C^1$ on $[-R,R]^3$, and there is a constant $C=C(a,R)$ such that $\|e\|_{C^1([-R,R]^3)}\le C\varepsilon$; in particular, with $\eta:=C\varepsilon$ assumed to satisfy $\eta\le1$, for all $(u,v,w)$

$$|e(u,v,w)|\le\eta,\qquad |\partial_ve(u,v,w)|\le\eta,\qquad |\partial_ue(u,v,w)|\le\eta,\qquad |\partial_we(u,v,w)|\le\eta ;$$

2. for every $(u,w)\in[-R,R]^2$ and each sign $s\in\{-1,+1\}$ the equation $P_{u,w}(v)=0$ has exactly one solution $v=M_s(u,w)$ with $s\,v\in[l,R]$, and this solution satisfies the margins

$$s\,M_s(u,w)-l\ge\tfrac34,\qquad R-s\,M_s(u,w)\ge\tfrac34 ;$$

moreover $M_s$ is of class $C^1$ on $[-R,R]^2$ with

$$\bigl|\partial_uM_s\bigr|\le d:=\frac{1+\eta}{2l-\eta},\qquad \bigl|\partial_wM_s\bigr|\le d ;$$

3. with $d$ as above and $\theta:=1/2$ one has, for every $a\ge100$ and $\eta\le1$,

$$d\le\frac2{13},\qquad 2d\le\frac4{13}<1,\qquad d\bigl(\theta+\theta^{-1}\bigr)\le\frac5{13}<1,\qquad \frac{d}{1-d\theta}\le\frac16<\frac23 .$$

4. **(orbit form of the root equation)** for all $(u,v,w)\in[-R,R]^3$,

$$P_{u,w}(v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B\bigl(u,V(u,v)\bigr)=V(v,w).$$
items.strategy: Estimate the C^1 norm of the defect from the inverse-branch bounds, compare the quadratic endpoints with the unperturbed signs to locate a root by the intermediate value theorem, and differentiate the defining equation to bound the partial derivatives; the numerical inequalities are verified at a=100 and monotonicity in eta.

items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#4 (the perturbed horseshoe, coding, chaos transfer, cones and transversality)
items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$ and put

$$R:=\sqrt a+3,\qquad l:=\sqrt a-3\ge7,\qquad \mathcal Q:=[-R-1,R+1]^2,\qquad \Sigma(x,y):=(y,x).$$

Let $C=C(a,R)$ be the constant of [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]], let $0<\varepsilon\le1/6$ with $\eta:=C\varepsilon\le1$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be open with $\mathcal Q\subseteq U$. Let $G=(A,B):U\to\mathbb R^2$ be a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto its image whose components satisfy, on $\mathcal Q$,

$$|A(x,y)-y|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_xA(x,y)|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_yA(x,y)-1|\le\varepsilon,$$

$$|B(x,y)-(y^2-a-x)|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_xB(x,y)+1|\le\varepsilon,\quad |\partial_yB(x,y)-2y|\le\varepsilon,$$

and assume in addition that $H:=\Sigma\circ G^{-1}\circ\Sigma$ is defined and of class $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $\mathcal Q$ and satisfies the same six inequalities on $\mathcal Q$ with the same constant $\varepsilon$. For each sign $u$ let $M_u$ be the root map of [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]] applied to $G$, let $V$ be the inverse branch of [[lem-close-map-first-component-has-uniform-inverse]], and let $M^H_u,V^H$ be the corresponding objects for $H$.

For a nonzero real $x$, write $\operatorname{sign}x:=+1$ if $x>0$ and
$\operatorname{sign}x:=-1$ if $x<0$; the sequence coordinates used below are
nonzero because their absolute values are at least $l\ge7$. Then:

1. **(coding)** for every $s\in X_\pm$ there is exactly one $q(s)\in B_R$ with $q_n(s)=M_{s_n}\bigl(q_{n-1}(s),q_{n+1}(s)\bigr)$ for all $n\in\mathbb Z$; it satisfies $l\le|q_n(s)|\le R$, $\operatorname{sign}q_n(s)=s_n$ and $R-|q_n(s)|\ge\tfrac34$, $|q_n(s)|-l\ge\tfrac34$; setting $v_n(s):=V(q_n(s),q_{n+1}(s))$ and

$$z_n(s):=\bigl(q_n(s),v_n(s)\bigr),\qquad h_G(s):=z_0(s)=\bigl(q_0(s),V(q_0(s),q_1(s))\bigr),$$

one has $G(z_n(s))=z_{n+1}(s)$ for all $n$;
2. **(conjugacy and chaos)** $h_G$ is a continuous bijection of $(X_\pm,D_\pm)$ onto $\Lambda_G:=h_G(X_\pm)$; granting the Axiom of Countable Choice (used once through the equivalence between closed and sequentially closed subsets of $\mathbb R^2$), it is a homeomorphism, and $G\circ h_G=h_G\circ S_\pm$, so $\Lambda_G$ is $G$-invariant. The set $\Lambda_G$ is sequentially compact and is compact under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega+\mathrm{DC}$. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, $G|_{\Lambda_G}$ is continuous, topologically mixing, and has dense periodic points; it is sensitive with sensitivity constant $2l$. Hence under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ it is chaotic in the stated sense.
3. **(fixed points)** for each sign $u$ the constant code $\bar u$ gives a fixed point $z_{\bar u}:=h_G(\bar u)=\bigl(\rho_u,V(\rho_u,\rho_u)\bigr)$, where $\rho_u=M_u(\rho_u,\rho_u)$ is the unique element of $u\,[l,R]$ with $\rho_u=M_u(\rho_u,\rho_u)$; these two fixed points are hyperbolic;
4. **(transverse homoclinic points)** let $s\in X_\pm$ be nonconstant with $s_n=u$ for $|n|\ge N$. Then $z_*:=h_G(s)\ne z_{\bar u}$, and there are $C^1$ curves $\gamma_s,\gamma_u:(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\to\mathbb R^2$ with $\gamma_s(0)=\gamma_u(0)=z_*$, $\gamma_s\bigl((-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\bigr)\subseteq W^s_G(z_{\bar u})$, $\gamma_u\bigl((-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\bigr)\subseteq W^u_G(z_{\bar u})$, tangent vectors $\gamma_s'(0)\in C^s_{3/4}$, $\gamma_u'(0)\in C^u_{3/4}$; since $C^s_{3/4}\cap C^u_{3/4}=\{0\}$ the tangent lines are distinct, so $z_*$ is a transverse homoclinic point of $z_{\bar u}$ ([[def-stable-unstable-cones-and-line-slopes]]).

items.title: The smooth $P$-periodic pulsed oscillator: the normalized pulse, its Hamiltonian and its stroboscopic (period) map
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#5 (the smooth P-periodic beta_delta, the Hamiltonian H_delta and its period map)
items.statement:
**The normalized pulse.** By [[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]], applied to $K=\{1/2\}\subset(0,1)$, choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $1/2$. Thus there are $0<\alpha<\beta<1$ with $\chi=1$ on $[\alpha,\beta]$. The continuous function $\chi$ is integrable on $[0,1]$; by additivity and monotonicity of the integral and the integral of a constant,

$$I:=\int_0^1\chi(s)\,ds\ge\int_\alpha^\beta\chi(s)\,ds=\beta-\alpha>0,$$

using integrability of continuous functions ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]), additivity and monotonicity ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]), and the integral of a constant ([[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]]).

Define $w_0:=\chi/I$ on $(0,1)$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be its extension by zero outside $(0,1)$. Since $\chi$ has compact support in $(0,1)$, this zero extension is smooth and compactly supported in $(0,1)$. Linearity of the integral ([[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]) gives

$$w\in C_c^\infty\bigl((0,1)\bigr),\qquad w\ge0,\qquad \int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1.$$

Fix such a pulse $w$ for the constructions below. The resulting coefficient and endpoint maps may depend on this choice; the later estimates apply to every such $w$, with constants allowed to depend on it.

**The periodic pulse.** Fix a real parameter $a\ge100$ and a smallness parameter $\delta>0$, and put $P:=\pi/2+\delta$. Define $\beta_\delta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ to be the $P$-periodic function whose restriction to $[0,P]$ is

$$\beta_\delta(t):=0\quad\Bigl(t\in\Bigl[0,\tfrac\pi2\Bigr]\Bigr),\qquad \beta_\delta(t):=\frac1\delta\,w\Bigl(\frac{t-\pi/2}{\delta}\Bigr)\quad\Bigl(t\in\Bigl[\tfrac\pi2,P\Bigr]\Bigr).$$

Both definitions use the same zero extension $w:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, so the endpoint values $w(0)$ and $w(1)$ are defined and equal to $0$. Since $w$ vanishes on neighborhoods of $0$ and $1$, all its derivatives vanish there; the $P$-periodic extension of $\beta_\delta$ is therefore of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Also $\beta_\delta\ge0$. To verify its normalization, put

$$B_\delta(t):=\begin{cases}0,&0\le t\le\pi/2,\\[2pt]\displaystyle\int_0^{(t-\pi/2)/\delta}w(s)\,ds,&\pi/2\le t\le P.\end{cases}$$

The integral function of the continuous $w$ has derivative $w$ by [[thm-ftc-first-part]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule]]) gives $B_\delta'(t)=\beta_\delta(t)$ on the pulse interval. Since $w$ vanishes near its endpoints, $B_\delta$ is differentiable across $t=\pi/2$ as well. Since $\beta_\delta$ is continuous and therefore integrable on $[0,P]$, the second part of the fundamental theorem ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]) gives

$$\int_0^P\beta_\delta(t)\,dt=B_\delta(P)-B_\delta(0)=\int_0^1w(s)\,ds=1.$$

**The Hamiltonian and its equations.** Use the phase domain $U=\mathbb R^2$
with coordinates $(q,p)$ and standard symplectic form $\omega=dq\wedge dp$
and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, as in
[[def-cm-phase-domain-and-standard-symplectic-two-form]]. For each fixed time
$t$, define the smooth Hamiltonian function

$$\mathcal H_\delta:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad \mathcal H_\delta(t,q,p):=\frac{p^2+q^2}{2}+\beta_\delta(t)\Bigl(aq-\frac{q^3}{3}\Bigr).$$

The Hamiltonian-vector-field convention is $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$, for
which [[prop-cm-hamiltonian-field-and-poisson-bracket-in-a-phase-chart]] gives
$X_H=J\nabla H=(\partial_pH,-\partial_qH)$. Here
$\partial_p\mathcal H_\delta=p$ and
$\partial_q\mathcal H_\delta=q+\beta_\delta(t)(a-q^2)$, so the associated
time-dependent first-order system is

$$q'=p,\qquad p'=-q+\beta_\delta(t)\,(q^2-a),$$

equivalently the second-order equation $q''=-q+\beta_\delta(t)(q^2-a)$; the right-hand side is $C^\infty$ in $(t,q,p)$, hence continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, so every initial condition has a unique maximal solution ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], [[def-maximal-ode-solution]], [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]). The system is $P$-periodic in $t$.

**Free rotation and pulse endpoint maps.** Over the first subinterval $[0,\pi/2]$ the pulse vanishes and the system is the free oscillator; define the **free rotation**

$$R_0:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad R_0(q,p):=(p,-q),$$

which is the time-$\pi/2$ solution operator of $q'=p$, $p'=-q$: the map $t\mapsto(q_0\cos t+p_0\sin t,\,-q_0\sin t+p_0\cos t)$ solves the free system by the derivative identities of sine and cosine ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]]) and has initial data $(q_0,p_0)$. Moreover $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ by the zero-set statement ([[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]), $\sin(\pi/2)>0$ by positivity on $(0,\pi)$ ([[cor-pi-is-the-first-positive-sine-zero]]), and $\sin^2(\pi/2)+\cos^2(\pi/2)=1$ ([[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]), so $\sin(\pi/2)=1$. Uniqueness of solutions then identifies the endpoint map with $R_0$.

For $s\in[0,1]$ the **rescaled pulse equation** is

$$q_s=\delta\,p,\qquad p_s=-\delta\,q+w(s)\,(q^2-a),$$

obtained from the second half of the period by the substitution $s=(t-\pi/2)/\delta$. For each initial state $z=(q,p)\in\mathbb R^2$, let $J_z^\delta$ be the open maximal interval containing $0$ of its solution to the rescaled equation. Define

$$D_\delta:=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:[0,1]\subseteq J_z^\delta\},\qquad K_\delta:D_\delta\to\mathbb R^2,\quad K_\delta(z):=(q(1),p(1)),$$

where $(q(s),p(s))$ is the unique maximal solution with $(q,p)(0)=z$ ([[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]]). For the original $P$-periodic system, let $J_z$ be the maximal existence interval of the solution through $z$ at time $0$, and set $D_P:=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:[0,P]\subseteq J_z\}$. Define the stroboscopic map by

$$G_\delta:D_{G_\delta}\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad D_{G_\delta}:=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:R_0(z)\in D_\delta\},\qquad G_\delta(z):=K_\delta(R_0(z)).$$

The change of time variable $s=(t-\pi/2)/\delta$ identifies solutions on $[\pi/2,P]$ with solutions of the rescaled equation on $[0,1]$. Concatenating with the unique free solution on $[0,\pi/2]$ shows $D_{G_\delta}=D_P$ and $G_\delta=\theta_P$ there, where $\theta_P:D_P\to\mathbb R^2$ is the stroboscopic map of [[def-cm-stroboscopic-map]]. Conversely, restricting any solution through time $P$ to the pulse interval and applying the same change of variables gives a solution of the rescaled equation through $s=1$; uniqueness identifies both maps.

items.title: The rescaled pulse endpoint map converges to the kick $K(q,p)=(q,p+q^2-a)$ in $C^1$, and the period map is smooth, symplectic and $C^1$-close to $F$
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#5 (the C^1 approximation of the pulse endpoint map by the kick, symplecticity, and G_delta -> F)
items.statement:
Fix $a\ge100$, put $R:=\sqrt a+3\ge13$, $S:=[-R-1,R+1]^2$, and let $w$, $\delta$, $P$, $\beta_\delta$, $R_0$, the rescaled pulse equation, the endpoint map $K_\delta$ and the stroboscopic map $G_\delta=K_\delta\circ R_0$ be as in [[def-smooth-periodic-oscillator-pulse-model]]. Let

$$K(q,p):=(q,\,p+q^2-a),\qquad F(q,p):=(p,\,p^2-a-q),\qquad J:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},$$

so that $F=K\circ R_0$. Then there are constants $\delta_1>0$ and $C_1<\infty$ depending only on $a$ and $w$ such that for every $0<\delta\le\delta_1$:

1. **(existence on the pulse)** for every $(q,p)\in S$ the solution of the rescaled equation with initial data $(q,p)$ exists on $[0,1]$ and stays in the compact tube $T:=[-R-2,R+2]\times[-M,M]$, $M:=R+1+(R+1)^2+1$; hence $K_\delta$ is defined on $S$, $K_\delta(S)\subseteq T$, and

$$\sup_{S}\bigl(|K_\delta-K|+\|DK_\delta-DK\|\bigr)\le C_1\delta$$

for the Euclidean norm and the operator norm;
2. **(closeness of the period map)** $\sup_S\bigl(|G_\delta-F|+\|DG_\delta-DF\|\bigr)\le C_1\delta$;
3. **(smoothness, invertibility, symplecticity)** $G_\delta$ is of class $C^\infty$ on an open neighbourhood $N$ of $S$; $DG_\delta(z)$ is invertible for every $z\in N$ and $G_\delta$ is injective on $N$, so $G_\delta:N\to G_\delta(N)$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism onto its image; and

$$DG_\delta(z)^{\mathsf T}J\,DG_\delta(z)=J\qquad(z\in N),$$

that is, $G_\delta$ is symplectic;
4. **(the reverse-conjugated map)** let $S_w(q,p):=(p,q)$ and $H_\delta:=S_w\circ G_\delta^{-1}\circ S_w$ on a neighbourhood of $S$. Then $H_\delta$ is of class $C^\infty$ there, and there is $C_2<\infty$, depending only on $a$ and $w$, with

$$\sup_{S}\bigl(|H_\delta-F|+\|DH_\delta-DF\|\bigr)\le C_2\delta .$$

Consequently, each of the six componentwise closeness inequalities for $G_\delta$ and $H_\delta$ holds on $S$ with common bound $\bar C\delta$, where $\bar C:=\max(C_1,C_2)$: each coordinate difference is bounded by the Euclidean norm, and each derivative-entry difference is bounded by the operator norm.

items.title: Explicit constants at $a=100$: the contraction factor, the fixed points $r_\pm$ and the constant-code solutions
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#1 (numerical evaluation of the constants at a=100 and the constant codes)
items.statement:
Take $a=100$ in [[lem-coded-quadratic-recurrence-is-a-contraction]], so that

$$R=\sqrt{100}+3=13,\qquad L=\sqrt{a-2R}=\sqrt{74},\qquad \sqrt{a+2R}=\sqrt{126}.$$

Then $126<169=13^2$, so $\sqrt{126}<R=13$; $74>1$, so $L>1$; and the contraction constant of $T_s$ on $B_{13}$ is

$$\frac1L=\frac1{\sqrt{74}}<1 .$$

The constant codes $\bar u$ ($u=\pm1$) are solved by the constant sequences $x_n=r_u$ with

$$11<r_+=1+\sqrt{101}<12,\qquad -10<r_-=1-\sqrt{101}<-9,$$

the two displayed bounds hold because $100<101<121$; and both satisfy the exact identity $r_u^2=100+2r_u$. Every coded sequence has $|x_n|\ge\sqrt{74}$, and its sign is the corresponding symbol.

items.title: The constant-code slope transform at $a=100$: the invariant slope of $h\mapsto1/(2r_+-h)$ and the cone constants

items.statement:
Take $a=100$, so $L=\sqrt{74}$, $k=1/2$, and let $r_+=1+\sqrt{101}$ be the constant-code value of the all-$+1$ code. The fixed slope of the forward transform $\Phi_y(h)=1/(2y-h)$ at $y=r_+$ is the small root of $h=1/(2r_+-h)$, i.e. of

$$h^2-2r_+h+1=0:\qquad h=r_+-\sqrt{r_+^2-1}=\frac1{r_++\sqrt{r_+^2-1}},$$

and one has $0<h<1/2$. Moreover $\lambda=2L-k=2\sqrt{74}-\tfrac12>1$ and $\Phi_{r_+}$ maps $[-1/2,1/2]$ into $[-\lambda^{-1},\lambda^{-1}]\subseteq[-1/2,1/2]$ with Lipschitz constant $\lambda^{-2}<1/2$.

items.title: The single-flip code at $a=100$: a nonperiodic coded orbit converging to the fixed point at both ends
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#1 (finite-word codes and their homoclinic limits)
items.statement:
Take $a=100$ and let $s\in X_\pm$ be the code with

$$s_0=-1,\qquad s_n=+1\ (n\ne0),$$

the single-flip code. Then $s$ is constant outside a finite set (indeed outside $\{0\}$), is not the constant code $\bar{+1}$, and is not periodic: $S_\pm^m s\ne s$ for every $m\ge1$, because the unique coordinate at which $S_\pm^ms$ equals $-1$ is $-m\ne0$ whereas $s$ equals $-1$ only at $0$. Consequently the coded point $z:=h(s)$ satisfies $z\ne(r_+,r_+)$ and $F^m(z)\ne z$ for every $m\ge1$, while

$$F^n(z)\longrightarrow(r_+,r_+)\quad(n\to+\infty\ \text{and}\ n\to-\infty).$$

items.title: The $\delta=0$ endpoint computation: the free rotation $(q,p)\mapsto(p,-q)$, the kick $(q,p)\mapsto(q,p+q^2-a)$ and $K\circ R_0=F$
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#5 (the explicit delta=0 endpoint computation)
items.statement:
In the model of [[def-smooth-periodic-oscillator-pulse-model]]:

1. the free oscillator $q'=p$, $p'=-q$ on the interval $[0,\pi/2]$ carries the initial data $(q_0,p_0)$ to

$$(q,p)\Bigl(\tfrac\pi2\Bigr)=\bigl(q_0\cos\tfrac\pi2+p_0\sin\tfrac\pi2,\;-q_0\sin\tfrac\pi2+p_0\cos\tfrac\pi2\bigr)=(p_0,-q_0)=R_0(q_0,p_0);$$

2. the $\delta=0$ rescaled equation $q_s=0$, $p_s=w(s)(q^2-a)$ has the exact solution $q(s)=q_0$, $p(s)=p_0+(q_0^2-a)\int_0^sw$, so its endpoint map is

$$K(q_0,p_0)=\bigl(q_0,\;p_0+q_0^2-a\bigr)$$

because $\int_0^1w=1$; and

$$(K\circ R_0)(q_0,p_0)=K(p_0,-q_0)=\bigl(p_0,\,-q_0+p_0^2-a\bigr)=F(q_0,p_0).$$

Moreover $\beta_\delta\ge0$ with $\int_0^P\beta_\delta=1$ and the pulse is supported in $(\pi/2,P)$.
items.strategy: Solve the two explicit linear ODEs by the sine/cosine addition formulas and evaluate at the endpoint times; no numerical integration is involved.

items.title: Explicit root margins at $a=100$: endpoint signs $25$ and $43$, and $d=2/13$ for $\eta=1$
items.reference: mechanical-horseshoe.md#4 (worked root bounds at the explicit parameter a=100)
items.statement:
Take $a=100$ in [[lem-perturbed-scalar-recurrence-root-bounds]], so that $R=13$, $l=7$, and suppose the defect bound is $\eta=1$. Then:

1. for all $u,w\in[-13,13]$ the unperturbed quadratic $v^2-100-u-w$ satisfies

$$v^2-100-u-w\Big|_{v=7}\le49-100+26=-25,\qquad v^2-100-u-w\Big|_{v=13}\ge169-100-26=43,$$

so the signs at the endpoints are strictly opposite with margins $25$ and $43$;
2. the derivative bound is $d=(1+\eta)/(2l-\eta)=(1+1)/(14-1)=2/13$, and

$$2d=\frac4{13}<1,\qquad d\Bigl(\frac12+2\Bigr)=\frac5{13}<1,\qquad \frac d{1-d/2}=\frac{2/13}{12/13}=\frac16<\frac23;$$

3. the root margins are at least $24/27>3/4$ and $42/27>3/4$, since the slope of $P_{u,w}$ is bounded by $2R+\eta=27$ on $[7,13]$.
